label: known
name: Platonic cosmic receptacle
mech: The dodecahedron, the Platonic solid tied to the cosmos, was made in Gaul and Britain as a material "receptacle" in Pythagorean-Platonic spirit, a philosophy Druids were said to admire. The twelve pentagonal faces embody the universe; holes and knobs are decorative or ritual variation, hence no standard sizes. A rod-shaped bone object beside the Gellep grave specimen suggests staff mounting, like a scepter of spiritual authority. Absence from Italy follows from its Celtic provincial origin.
value: It explains the geography, lack of wear, lack of standardisation and silence of texts. Proponents propose better-contexted finds and evidence of mounting.

label: known
name: Gallo-Roman divination and magic
mech: A private, non-official object of sorcery or fortune-telling, absent from literature and art because unofficial. Twelve faces echo zodiac or twelve-oracle systems like the Sortes Sangallenses and the zodiac-named Geneva die. In the Spindle-of-Necessity version, thread was wound across knobs and through holes to cast or read fate. Breakage and repair of finds such as Kortessem may mark ritual destruction.
value: It explains absence from texts, lack of wear and the Celtic-area distribution. Its test is thread or fibre traces on knobs and holes, and deposition patterns showing deliberate burial or breakage.

label: known
name: Farmer's sowing-date instrument
mech: Aimed at the sun and steadied on its knobs, opposite holes of different diameters act as apertures whose sunlight geometry marks the equinoxes and the autumn window for sowing winter wheat. Different hole pairs correspond to different dates or latitudes, which is why dimensions vary. It needed no markings, being a calendar-by-light.
value: It explains twelve differently sized holes, northern farming provinces and low wear (used a few days a year). Wagemans tested a bronze copy over several years at different latitudes.

label: known
name: Wax-forming tool
mech: Warm wax pressed into the hollow body through the holes forms discrete, repeatable wax elements, such as bullae securing cords or marking documents. Corner knobs act as spacers during compression and aid removal; aperture size controls thickness and the raised central boss. The tool turns a flexible craft action into a standard one.
value: It explains knobs, variable holes and the single wax-bearing specimen. Lamb's plastic trials produced repeatable forms; the proposed test is bronze replicas, wax-residue analysis and matching ancient sealings.

label: known
name: Coincidence rangefinder
mech: Looking through a face's small hole at a standard-sized object (a man, a standard, a pole) until it exactly fills the large opposite hole gives distance by proportion. The faces form pairs of differing diameters, giving a range of calibrated distances; knobs let it rest flat or be gripped. Finds at forts link it to military engineering or surveying, like the dioptra.
value: It explains the opposite-hole size contrast and finds in military camps. Sparavigna's test is measuring hole-pair ratios against plausible target sizes and ranges on real objects.

label: g1_crux
name: Axle-spun lot, size-coded holes
mech: A household oracle was threaded on an upright wooden or bone rod through the larger unringed opposite pair, which were its bearings. It was spun and read from whichever ringed hole stopped facing the consultant. The answer was that hole's size, so each object needs ten distinguishable diameters, never a scheme shared with others, and no letters. Rings frame the readable apertures; knobs give spinning grip and keep rims off surfaces. Soft rods and occasional private Gallo-British use leave bronze unworn and suit settlement finds and textual silence; the Gellep bone rod is its axle.
value: It alone makes within-object variation, no cross-object scheme, no inscriptions and the unringed pair all necessary. In Guggenberger's per-object measurements, if type-2a unringed pairs are often unequal or ringed holes on one object coincide within 0.5 mm, it is refuted.

label: g1_crux
name: Hand-tuned bronze vessel whistle
mech: Each piece was a Gallo-British edge-blown vessel flute: the player blew across one larger unringed hole, its opposite twin was a thumb vent, and the ring-marked holes were finger or wax stops. Pitch depends on open hole area against cavity volume, so graded holes give a fuller scale, and continuously varying bodies forced individual tuning, which rules out any shared hole standard. Knobs let it be held and set down without blocking holes. Wax, used to join and tune ancient pan-pipes, explains the German residue; lips and fingers leave bronze unworn; and the Kortessem repair restores airtightness.
value: It turns differing holes, continuous sizes, the unringed pair and the wax trace into requirements. Sound the intact Norton Disney piece with an artificial-mouth air jet across an unringed rim, other holes film-sealed: if no stable tone results, it is refuted.

label: g1_crux
name: Hole-signature membership token
mech: Each was a recognition token of a non-official Gallo-British association, its hole diameters a personal signature checked against a counterpart such as a pegged wooden gauge. A signature must vary within each object and never repeat between objects, exactly the observed pattern; the larger unringed opposite pair fixes the reference axis so the ten ringed sizes are read in order. Knobs and rings make imitation costly; shown rather than used, it stays unworn and uninscribed, while unofficial membership explains textual silence and spread from Gaul to Britain and beyond the frontier. Tokens followed owners into graves, hoards and rivers.
value: It makes the missing shared size scheme a design requirement and fits extra-imperial spread and valued deposition. Measure hole roundness on existing pieces: if scatter within single holes equals the steps between holes on one object, no signature exists and it is refuted.

label: g1_mech
name: Staff finial on tapering shaft
mech: A light insignia head was slid onto a staff through the larger unringed opposite pair and wedged where the taper met that pair's smaller hole, so opposite pairs may differ widely. Ringed holes faced outward as decorated windows; knobs were ornamental terminals shielding the head when grounded. Each head fitted its own staff, so no size scheme was needed. Carried occasionally, it stayed unworn, followed its holder into graves (the Gellep rod), hoards or rivers, and as an unofficial regional badge escaped texts and art.
value: It makes the unringed axis and unequal opposite pairs necessary, which symbolic and instrument readings leave unexplained. Under CT and microscopy, type-2a unringed pairs showing no more rim abrasion, organic traces or staining than ringed holes, or admitting no single tapering rod, refute it.

label: g1_mech
name: Touch-coded casting lot
mech: Tossed onto cloth, it tumbles on its knobs and settles with one face up. That face is read by its hole (size, ringed or not; the large unringed pair a distinct outcome), legible by eye or finger, so no letters were needed, and since each owner knew their own piece, neither a shared scheme nor fairness mattered. A light shell landing on cloth wears little. It belongs to north-western lot-casting (Tacitus describes Germanic lots thrown onto a white cloth), not Mediterranean dice culture, fitting distribution, civil and grave contexts and textual silence.
value: It explains why holes differ within each object yet share no scheme between objects, and why nothing is inscribed. On 10+ pieces, microscope knob tips against protected recesses: repeated tumbling polishes tips, so tips as fresh as recesses refute it.

label: g1_mech
name: Fumigation cage for aromatics
mech: Resin or herbs on a small ember went in through the largest hole; then it sat on a smaller-holed face, ember over that hole. Knobs lift it to admit air while upper holes vent smoke, and turning it to another face changes intake and smoulder rate, so holes needed only to differ within a piece; rings are ornament. The thin shell heats fast, knobs give cooler grips, use causes no wear, and the wax specimen is residue. Domestic, bath, theatre and funerary fumigation fits the mixed contexts, a regional form of a common rite, unnamed in texts.
value: It explains knobs as stand-offs, the perforated hollow and the wax specimen together, which symbolic and instrument readings do not. Clean interiors on 10+ pieces, with no soot, charred resin or heat tint and no resin markers by GC-MS, refute it.

label: g1_neg
name: Bronze serpent's-egg talisman
mech: Pliny (NH 29.52) describes the anguinum, a Gaulish Druid badge, apple-sized with a cupped crust, carried to win lawsuits, often identified as a fossil sea urchin. The dodecahedron copies that urchin in bronze: pentagons give its five-fold symmetry, ten ringed holes its ten zones of ringed tubercles, the larger unringed opposite pair its mouth and anus, knobs its spine bosses. Smiths copied freely, so sizes vary. A private charm of a suppressed priesthood stays unworn, unlettered, unpictured and concentrated in Gaul, Britain and the Rhineland, ending in houses, graves, rivers and hoards.
value: It explains the ten-plus-two layout, rings, knobs and Gallo-British distribution together, which rivals treat separately. Test: in Guggenberger's per-object tables, the five ringed holes around one unringed pole should differ systematically from the five around the other (urchin underside versus top); no difference refutes it.

label: g1_neg
name: Founder's hollow-casting masterpiece
mech: Casting a closed polyhedron hollow with millimetre walls is among the hardest lost-wax tasks; the dodecahedron was a provincial founder's proof piece, kept or given to patrons. Every face is holed because the clay core must be pinned and raked out: the larger, unringed, sometimes oval opposite pair is the main core-pin axis, filed open, while the other ten got finishing rings. Corner knobs are feeders filling thin junctions; each founder set his own core and wax, so sizes vary. Display means no wear or lettering; graves, hoards and the Kortessem repair show value; the range maps a north-western casting tradition.
value: It explains why every face is holed, why one pair is larger and unringed, the knobs and the thin walls, all arbitrary in use-based readings. Test: radiograph existing pieces; if core-pin, filing and porosity traces do not concentrate on the larger unringed axis, it is refuted.

label: g1_neg
name: Travelling founders' trade sample
mech: Itinerant founders, casting on site for towns, villas and forts, carried a dodecahedron as proof they could cast closed, thin-walled hollows. Its form records casting: holes pin and empty the core, the larger unringed pair marks the main core axis, ringed holes display finishing, knobs fed thin corners; each team cast its own, so sizes vary. Seldom handled, samples show little wear and needed no words; they were lost at work sites, rivers, wells and pits, sold on into graves and hoards, and taken beyond the frontier by hired teams. Fixed Mediterranean workshops needed none.
value: It explains the civil majority, military minority, river and pit losses and Slovak finds as one trade's itinerary, not a cult or army. Test: pXRF and core-clay analysis should show a few alloy-clay groups each spread over hundreds of kilometres; local matches at each findspot refute it.

label: g2_evo
name: Post-Druidic yes-or-no lot
mech: Lay Gaulish diviners, like the Historia Augusta's 3rd-century "dryades" (one at Tongeren), threw it; it rests on five knobs, one axis vertical. If the unringed ovals form that axis, a wide window opens through: "yes", one throw in six; ringed faces all mean "no", so sizes may repeat. Druidic lore was unwritten (Caesar, Gallic War 6.14), and banned Druidic sacrifice left former Druidic lands needing a bloodless lot until Christianisation.
value: It derives map, dates, missing letters and household contexts from a tradition absent around the Mediterranean. Knob tips no more polished than protected recesses on 10+ pieces refute it.

label: g2_evo
name: Bright-or-dark day-luck lot
mech: Thrown on pale cloth, it rests on knobs, one opposite pair vertical; the reader looks down through the top hole. A larger lower hole shows only bright cloth, "good"; a smaller one, a dark interior ring, "not good"; near-equal pairs void the throw, so no shared scheme is needed. It extended to single decisions the good/not-good (MAT/ANM) day-marking of Gaul's 2nd-century Coligny calendar, used only in Celtic-calendar lands until Christian reckoning.
value: It makes variable opposite pairs and missing letters requirements, and ties the map to Gaulish time-reckoning. Measured opposite pairs (Jublains, Guggenberger's list) mostly equal within 1 mm refute it.

label: g2_evo
name: Tallow-candle draught shade
mech: A home-dipped tallow candle passed up through whichever hole fitted its thickness, its foot on the table between the knobs; the flame burned draught-proof inside, the opposite hole venting smoke. Graded holes suit irregular candles, so no shared scheme was needed; the unringed core openings admitted a light, and rings mark designed holes. North of the olive line Baetican lamp oil dwindled after c. 200, making candles the light until c. 400.
value: It derives hole range, knobs, scarce wax (tallow was normal) and map from lighting economics. Rims and interiors of 10+ pieces lacking both animal-fat lipids (GC-MS) and soot refute it.

label: g2_evo
name: Festival ember carrier
mech: Yearly, in the Celtic custom (recorded later in Ireland) of quenching hearths and rekindling them from a sanctuary fire, each household carried a live coal home in it. The coal entered an unringed core opening; turning the shell set a larger or smaller ringed vent (rings mark designed vents) windward to keep it glowing, knobs giving cooler grips. Coligny's Samonios month attests this festival calendar in 2nd-century Gaul; Christianisation ended it.
value: It derives household contexts, annual (hence unworn) use and the Celtic-calendar map from one rite. Interiors of 10+ pieces without heat tint, soot or ash refute it.

label: g2_evo
name: Coursing hunter's personal whistle
mech: Blown across an unringed oval, all other holes open, it gives one note fixed by cavity volume and total hole area, so no hole is stopped by hand. Varying bodies and holes give each piece its own note for its owner's hounds to learn; a shared scheme would defeat that. Arrian (Cynegeticus, 2nd century) calls coursing with hounds a Celtic sport, unlike Mediterranean net-hunting, hence north-western villas and forts until c. 400.
value: It makes continuous size spread and no shared hole scheme necessary. Unringed rims on 10+ pieces as blunt as ringed ones, with no sharp blowing edge, refute it.

label: g2_evo
name: Sanctuary-theatre chorus pitch-giver
mech: At festivals in Gaul's and Britain's sanctuary theatres, a chorus leader gave the opening note by blowing across an unringed oval, other holes open. After casting, the maker reamed ringed holes wider until the piece gave its owner's note, so holes differ within every piece and follow no shared scheme; rings were layout lines. Choristers kept them at home, hence settlement finds; the temple closures of 391-392 ended them.
value: It explains within-piece differences and the missing scheme as tuning, tied to a regional building type. Ringed-hole walls on 10+ pieces without post-casting reaming marks refute it.

label: g2_evo
name: Native priest's radiate sceptre
mech: A short rod (as at Gellep) passed through the unringed core openings, so the ten ringed holes formed two radiating five-fold crowns, each holding a sacred-plant sprig; stems differed, hence varied holes and no shared scheme. Never grounded, it stayed unworn; knobs stopped it rolling on altars. Native priesthoods (Gaulish gutuatri; Romano-British priestly crowns and sceptres, known from finds, not images) existed only in the Celtic north-west and ended with the Theodosian bans.
value: It makes the unringed axis, the five-fold form and graded holes necessary and derives art's silence. Ringed rims on 10+ pieces without stem scratches or plant residue refute it.

label: g2_evo
name: Spring-cult lustral sprinkler
mech: On a short handle through the unringed core openings, the herb-packed head was dipped in a sacred spring, river or well and shaken, spraying from ten ringed outlets in two crowns; graded holes vary drop size, so no shared scheme mattered. Knobs let it stand to drain; water causes no wear. Celtic water cults flourished in 2nd-4th-century Gaul and Britain, hence river and well finds; Mediterranean lustration used a branch.
value: It explains river and well finds, handle axis and graded outlets together. Interiors of 10+ dry-land pieces lacking both plant micro-remains and water scale refute it.

label: final
name: Knob-footed twelve-face divination lot
mech: It was a bronze lot for private divination: the person consulting it threw it onto a cloth or table, it came to rest on the five knobs of one face, and the horizontal face opposite was read. Each face is told apart without letters by its hole (size class, ringed or not) and by where it sits relative to the larger unringed pair, which the specialists read as the casting-core axis and which serves as the pole. Because each piece carries its own code, holes differ within every object while no size scheme or module is shared between objects. The twelve outcomes stand for the twelve parts of the heavens: a 4th-century silver-coated lead dodecahedron from Geneva carries the twelve zodiac names in Latin, one per face, and is interpreted as a divination die, and Platonist tradition made the dodecahedron the figure of the whole cosmos (Timaeus 55c). The knobs are feet: only their tips touch the cloth, so the face to read is unambiguous and the ringed rims are spared. Owners were households and individuals across civil and military society, who treated the piece as a valuable; hence rich graves of both sexes, a coin hoard, shrine deposits, and the repair on the Kortessem piece. It was a regional product of the Gaulish, Rhenish and British bronze trade, which soldiers and traders carried to the Danube legionary bases; the Mediterranean cast lots with other devices (the oak lots of Praeneste, the 2nd-century knucklebone oracles of Asia Minor) and already knew both hollow lost-wax casting and the dodecahedron, so the map reflects a regional device, not a missing technique, and the type appears c. 150-200 while its 4th-century end coincides with imperial laws against divination (356-357) and pagan cult (391-392).
value: It is the only explanation that turns four hard facts into one function: holes that vary within each object, no shared scheme, no inscriptions, and the fixed twelve-face template. It also rests on a dated regional parallel (Geneva) instead of the misread Germanic lots. Still unexplained: why only the north-west used this device (shown only by the distribution and the single Geneva die), the start c. 150-200, any role for the knobs beyond feet, and the Arloff icosahedron with holes in only two faces. Decisive test: on 10 or more pieces with surviving original surface, compare all 20 knob tips with their bases, plus the hole rims and interior, by stereo microscope or 3D scan. Throwing predicts rounding on every tip, roughly evenly, with clean rims and interiors; tips as sharp as their bases, or wear limited to one face's five knobs or to particular rims, refute it.

label: final
name: Cosmic emblem, sometimes on a staff
mech: It was a devotional image of the cosmos, Plato's fifth figure that the god used "for the whole" (Timaeus 55c), owned by households and individuals of the north-western provinces rather than by priests. It was kept at home or in shrines, and sometimes carried on a short rod passed through the unringed core-axis pair; at Krefeld-Gellep a bone object, possibly a handle, lay beside the 4th-century piece in a rich woman's grave. It went with the dead, to sanctuaries (Lydney, Pfofeld) and into hoards. The form mattered, not a mechanism: the hollow knobbed icosahedron from Arloff has holes in only two opposite faces, so face holes were optional; rings and knobs are the ordinary decoration of provincial bronze; and hole sizes vary because nothing depended on them. It was rarely handled and never put to work, so it stayed largely unworn, and it needed no letters because the shape carried the meaning. Its region is that of a provincial taste in cult objects and a regional workshop network; the proposed Druid-Pythagorean root is weak, because the Druids were suppressed under Tiberius and Claudius, 150-300 years before the objects, and its end coincides with the closing of pagan cult in 391-392.
value: It accounts for the low wear, the rarity, the valuable and sacred contexts and the two-holed icosahedron better than the lot does, and it drops the reviewed failures of the priest's-sceptre version (priestly regalia, sprig crowns, knobs as anti-roll stops). But it leaves the hard fact of hole variation within each object, and the three preset hole classes at Jublains, as unexplained ornament, and its regional cause is unsupported. On the same test it predicts unworn knob tips, or wear only on the five knobs of one display face, plus abrasion or mineral-preserved wood or bone inside the unringed pair where it was mounted on a staff; evenly rounded tips on all 20 knobs refute it.

label: known_knit
name: Glove-finger knitting frame
mech: It was a knitting frame of the "knitting nancy" kind: yarn was looped round the five knobs that frame one face and lifted over them row by row, so a knitted tube grew down through that face's hole into the hollow body and out through the opposite hole. Each hole gives a tube of a different width, for fingers of different sizes, which is why the holes differ within every piece and between pieces; the knobs are the pegs, and the hollow body guides the tube. Gloves were needed in the cold north-western provinces, which is why the objects are found there and not around the Mediterranean.
value: It gives a working role to the knobs, the hollow body and the varied holes together, and links the distribution to climate. Polish on the knobs of the faces used, or textile fibre traces, would support it; knob surfaces as fresh as the recesses on pieces with original surface refute it.

label: h2r4
name: Bronze head on a rod
mech: The hollow bronze head was slid onto a wooden or bone rod through the two largest holes, the unringed opposite pair, which always lie on one axis; the thickest rod passes there (up to 22.6 mm on the Kleiner Feldberg piece) and a slightly tapering rod seats in both holes at once. On a vertical rod the viewer saw two crowns of five ringed faces and the 20 knobs; the rings and the differing sizes of the ten other holes were decoration, which is why their sizes form a continuum with no shared scheme. It was carried by men and women, mostly in civil settlements, rarely handled, and put into rich graves and hoards; at Krefeld-Gellep its position in a mid-4th-century woman's grave suggested a bone staff or handle. The twelve faces may stand for Plato's figure of the cosmos (Timaeus 55c), an argument from texts, not objects; why it occurs only in the north-west in the 2nd-4th centuries is not explained.
value: It explains the axial unringed pair of the largest holes, the rubbed-looking rims of that pair (Duval 1981 on the Vienne piece; the roughest rims on the Kleiner Feldberg scan, but the smoothest on the Hunt scan), the unworn knobs and the continuum of hole sizes, which a lot with a hole code does not. Decisive test: stereo microscope on the unringed rims of the Kleiner Feldberg and Hunt pieces; wear striations along the axis with clean ringed rims support it, rims showing only casting or file marks refute it.
